title: JSON Web Tokens (JWT) in ASP.NET Core

cards.title: Introduction to JWT
cards.content:
JSON Web Tokens (JWT) are an open standard (RFC 7519) that defines a compact and self-contained way for securely transmitting information between parties as a JSON object.

In ASP.NET Core, JWTs are heavily used for stateless authentication in Web APIs.

cards.title: Structure of a JWT
cards.content:
A JWT is divided into three parts separated by dots (.):

  • Header: Contains the token type and signing algorithm (e.g., HS256).
  • Payload: Contains the claims (user data, permissions, expiration).
  • Signature: Used to verify that the sender of the JWT is who it says it is and to ensure the message wasn't changed along the way.

pairs.right: Contains signing algorithm and token type

items.text: Client sends credentials (username/password) to the API.
API validates credentials and generates a signed JWT.
API returns the JWT in the response to the client.
Client stores JWT and sends it in the Authorization header for subsequent requests.

cards.title: Required NuGet Packages
cards.content:
To implement JWT authentication in ASP.NET Core, you need to install the JwtBearer NuGet package.

dotnet add package Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer

content.template: In Program.cs, you configure authentication using builder.Services.AddAuthentication(options => { options.DefaultAuthenticateScheme = JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme; }).AddJwtBearer(options => { options.TokenValidationParameters = new TokenValidationParameters { ValidateIssuer = true, ValidateAudience = true, IssuerSigningKey = new SymmetricSecurityKey(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(builder.Configuration["Jwt:Key"]!)); });

options.text: Claims represent statements about an entity (typically, the user) and additional metadata.
Claims are encrypted passwords stored in the database.
Claims are routing rules for ASP.NET Core controllers.

cards.title: Protecting Endpoints
cards.content:
Once configured, you can secure your Minimal APIs or Controllers using the [Authorize] attribute or extension methods.

[Authorize]
[HttpGet("secure-data")]
public IActionResult GetSecureData()
{
    return Ok("This is protected data.");
}

options.text: Store sensitive user passwords inside the JWT payload.
Keep token lifespans short and use refresh tokens for long-term sessions.
Always transmit JWT over HTTP instead of HTTPS.

cards.title: Conclusion
cards.content: You have learned how JWT works, its core structure (Header, Payload, Signature), how to configure it in ASP.NET Core via middleware, and how to protect API endpoints using the [Authorize] attribute.
